extracted.intended_audience: educators, school administrators, and policymakers interested in establishing or evaluating manual/technical training in schools
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for organizing, running, and justifying an elementary/secondary manual training (technical) school that integrates manual and intellectual education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with practical life / harmony with the busy world
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a lack of harmony between the school-house and the busy world that surrounds it; education should prepare students for real occupations and practical life rather than leaving them 'unfinished' or unready for work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If education is misdirected students may be unable to work and resort to fraud or violence; indiscriminate education that withdraws youth from certain occupations can crowd and degrade some employments while leaving others to foreigners, producing social disorder. Evaluate whether the curriculum connects school learning to the material world and to likely occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of multiple arts of expression (verbal, pictorial, mechanical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Next in rank to the ability to think deeply is the power to give clear and full expression to thoughts — by verbal (spoken/written), pictorial (drawing), and mechanic (making/prototype) arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each is 'a distinct language' and 'absolutely essential to modern civilization.' Example: inventor's idea poorly conveyed by words, improved by drawings, and perfected by a mechanic's working model. Schools should teach and value all three expression methods; assess whether students are trained in writing/speech, drawing (plans/elevations/sections), and hands-on making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete before abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: The concrete should precede the abstract: give children clear and accurate thoughts of real things (plants, animals, laws of materials, qualities then quantities) before venturing into abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought must precede expression; start with material, sensory, and practical experiences to form clear mental images. Evaluate lesson sequencing: are concrete experiences and objects used as the foundation for later abstract instruction?

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate clear thinking; avoid fogginess and over-scholaring
rubrics_metrics.description: Form habits of clear thinking; avoid stopping short with ill-defined results or resting content with obscure, half-grown mental images. Beware of straining attention by too much schooling, overtaxing the mind with too many/difficult subjects, and bad air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear thinking yields durable results even in abstract work; conversely, mental fogginess stultifies the mind. Assess workload, lesson difficulty, duration and school environment (ventilation, rest/recreation) to prevent mental and physical decrepitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced curriculum in five parallel lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The course of study should run through three years in five parallel lines: (1) a course in pure mathematics; (2) a course in science and applied mathematics; (3) a course in language and literature; (4) a course in penmanship and drawing; (5) a course in tool-work in woods and metals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to make each child a master of verbal, pictorial and mechanical arts of expression. Evaluate whether the school's curriculum includes these five strands and how they are integrated over the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of manual and intellectual education (organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer to incorporate manual with intellectual education under the name 'school' rather than separate 'school in morning, shop in afternoon' or purely factory-subordinate models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professor Thompson's classification of French plans (school in workshop; workshop in school; school and shop side by side; half-time schools) is cited; author favors incorporation and notes the St. Louis model differs by having full study/recitation rooms as well as shops. Evaluate organizational model: are manual and intellectual elements truly integrated, with dedicated facilities for both?

rubrics_metrics.name: Shop management: avoid manufacturing for sale / no income-driven shop
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not manufacture articles for sale in school shops; schools that rely on shop income are confined to salable work and cannot run systematic, progressive exercises for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a shop expects revenue, pupils will be kept doing what yields income and will not progress pedagogically. Anti-pattern: treating the shop as a business/apprenticeship rather than an instructional environment. Evaluate shop policies: are exercises chosen for pedagogical progression rather than marketability? Is the school funded sufficiently so instruction is not subordinated to making saleable goods?

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow trade training; teach underlying arts impartially
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confine lads strictly to learning a particular trade at school; a single trade is 'educationally very narrow' — teach the underlying arts which underlie many trades so students can move to a trade later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In monarchies strict trade grooves may work, but not in America where many trades exist. The school should develop general mechanical/artisan arts, leaving a 'step' to an actual trade. Evaluate whether instruction emphasizes general arts and adaptability rather than narrow, employer-directed tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic, progressive gradation of shop exercises with student-centered pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Shops should provide a systematic and progressive series of exercises; a student should be allowed to leave a step or process the moment he has fairly learned it rather than being kept at repetitive tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with common apprenticeship described as 'a drudge' where much time is wasted. Example: bright boy made faster, more rounded progress in a manual training school than he would as an apprentice. Evaluate whether the program sequences exercises in graded difficulty and permits mastery-based progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject self-supporting funding model for thorough education
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit that a good school for thorough education costs money and should not be run on the fallacy of being self-supporting (e.g., by manufacturing shop products or other commercial income).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: cannot run a full medical school or public school of oratory purely on income from services without compromising educational quality. Assess the school's funding model: does it rely on commercial shop income to the detriment of pedagogy?

rubrics_metrics.name: Shop lesson duration optimized (three-hour lessons recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Foley reports that three-hour lessons produce the best results: sufficient to create vigorous interest without tiring and produce more and better work than longer sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He tried four-hour days but found three hours optimal; use lesson length that balances physical stamina, attention, and lasting impression. Evaluate scheduling: are shop sessions arranged to optimize learning and avoid fatigue?

rubrics_metrics.name: Program parameters and facilities (age, course length, equipment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmatic choices matter: example — St. Louis Manual Training-School admits boys at fourteen (not fifteen), offers a three-year course (not two), and maintains full and independent equipment of study/recitation rooms as well as shops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These parameters (admission age, course duration, and dedicated facilities) are practical choices that affect outcomes. Evaluate whether the school's admission criteria, program length, and physical equipment align with pedagogical aims and allow integration of manual and intellectual training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrable outcomes: intellectual balance, mechanical judgment, and enduring skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual training should produce increased interest in practical affairs, 'a good mechanical judgment', level-headedness, and enduring manual skills useful across many callings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites parental testimonials (boys fixing sewing machines, mending chairs, making household articles) and instructors' reports on exercises (blacksmithing sequence, wood-work tracings). Evaluate programs by observable student outcomes: practical tasks completed, changes in disposition/interests, and instructor/judge commendations.
